title: Battle of White Horse Hill (1952): 10 Days, 24 Changes of Hands
subtitle: Oct 6 – 15, 1952

lines: October 1952. Cheorwon, Gangwon Province.
On a nameless hill just 395 meters high, two armies staked everything.
The Chinese command's math was simple.
Three times the men. Push hard, and the hill falls.

bubbles.text:
Three to one.
Push them off!

scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: In ten days, about 280,000 shells from both sides fell on this one hill.
The forest burned away, and the ridgeline was stripped bare and white.
In that time, the hill is said to have changed hands twenty-four times.

visual.big: A Hill That Changed Hands 24 Times

lines: On one side, the ROK 9th Infantry Division. On the other, the elite Chinese 38th Army.
The attackers outnumbered the defenders more than three to one.
And ten days later,
the men still standing on that hill were South Korean.

visual.text:
Ten days later,
who still held the hill?

lines: When the smoke cleared, the hill looked like a white horse lying down.
This is the battle that decided the fate of the Cheorwon plain: the Battle of White Horse Hill.
By 1952, the war was entering its third year.
The front had stalled near the 38th Parallel, as truce talks dragged on at Panmunjom.
Where the ceasefire line fell depended on who held the ground.
So both sides poured blood into every single hill.
At the center lay the so-called Iron Triangle, linking Cheorwon, Kimhwa, and Pyonggang.
The heart of the central front, where every major road met.
And northwest of the Cheorwon plain, a lone ridge looked down over the flatland.
On the maps, it carried only a number: Hill 395.
The plain around it sat at roughly 200 meters above sea level.
From this solitary peak, the entire Cheorwon area lay open below.
If it fell, the U.S. IX Corps would have to give up the Cheorwon area.
For the Chinese, it would open a road leading south.
The hill was entrusted to Major General Kim Jong-oh, commander of the ROK 9th Division.
On the first day of the war, he had held the North Koreans at Chuncheon for three days.
scenes.label: Maj. Gen. Kim Jong-oh (left) · 1954

lines: In 1951, the 9th Division had been rebuilt through a grueling retraining program.
Now, about 12,000 of its men faced their true test.
scenes.label: ROK troops training in U.S. style (Feb 1952)

lines: Their opponent was the Chinese 38th Army.
In the winter of 1950, Peng Dehuai was said to have hailed it with the words 'Long live the 38th Army.'
On October 3rd, a Chinese officer crossed over to the South Korean lines.
What he revealed was alarming: a full-scale assault on this hill was coming soon.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: The 9th Division ringed the hill with tanks, anti-aircraft guns, and searchlights.
Flares to turn night into day were piled high.
scenes.label: M46 tank with searchlight (Korean War)

lines: October 6th, 1952.
Chinese shells began to blanket Hill 395.
At the same time, the Chinese blew open the floodgates of the Pongnae reservoir to the north.
The swollen Yokkok Stream cut off the hill's rear, so ROK reinforcements could not cross.
As night fell, Chinese infantry swarmed the slopes to the sound of bugles and whistles.
When the front rank fell, the next rank climbed right over them.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: South Korean and American artillery laid a barrage in front of the hill with eighty-one guns.
On the first night alone, an estimated five hundred Chinese soldiers fell.
scenes.label: 155mm howitzer firing · near Kumhwa (Jun 1952)

lines: Around the same time, Chinese troops also massed against Hill 281, 'Arrowhead,' to the southeast.
The French Battalion holding it threw back every assault.
Control of the hill flipped between night and day.
By night the Chinese took it; by morning the South Koreans took it back.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: When ammunition ran out in the trenches, men fought hand to hand with bayonets and rifle butts.
Day by day, the soil on the hill turned the color of blood.
scenes.label: Wounded ROK soldier carried through a trench · Capital Hill (Sep 1952)

lines: On October 10th, at 4:30 in the morning, the hill was lost again.
But at 8:15 that same morning, South Korean troops took it back once more.
At the Hwarang Hill outpost, 23-year-old platoon leader 2nd Lt. Lee Seong-deok fought on, surrounded.
Out of ammunition and water, he held to the end, and was killed on October 7th.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: General Kim rotated his regiments into the fight, one after another.
When the 28th Regiment was spent, in went the 29th, and then the 30th.
Most counterattacks came at night.
Under the glare of flares, small platoons crawled up the ridgeline with grenades in hand.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: At first light, American fighter-bombers came screaming down from the sky.
More than 358 napalm bombs alone fell on and around the hill.
scenes.label: Napalm strike (Oct 1952)

lines: October 12th.
The 1st Battalion, 30th Regiment, moved out against the main peak, once again in Chinese hands.
First, U.S. artillery fired a 'Time on Target' strike, many batteries hitting one point at once.
Two Chinese battalions forming up to attack were wiped out where they stood.
scenes.label: 155mm 'Long Tom' firing at night (Korean War)

lines: But just below the summit, a single Chinese machine-gun bunker blocked the way.
Again and again, 1st Company's charges broke against it.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: Then 2nd Lt. Kang Seung-woo and two soldiers, Oh Gyu-bong and Ahn Young-kwon, stepped forward.
Clutching explosives and grenades, they threw themselves at the machine-gun nest.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: The bunker collapsed in a thunderous blast,
and the three men never came back.
In that opening, 1st Company charged all at once.
At 1:20 p.m., the main peak of Hill 395 was back in South Korean hands.
They are remembered as the 'Three Heroes of White Horse Hill.'

visual.sub: 2nd Lt. Kang Seung-woo · Oh Gyu-bong · Ahn Young-kwon

lines: What remained was Camel Ridge, northwest of the peak.
On the morning of October 14th, the 29th Regiment finally seized that ridge as well.
That night, the Chinese 38th Army finally pulled back.
Ten days of fighting for the hill had come to an end.
As the smoke lifted, people were stunned by what was left.
The forest was gone, and the stripped ridge looked like a white horse lying down.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: And so it got its name: 'Baengma-goji,' White Horse Hill.
Against an enemy three times its size, how did the ROK Army hold this hill?
Let's break it down into four factors.
First, they knew the attack was coming.
Thanks to the defector's warning, the 9th Division had three days to fortify the hill.
What might have been a surprise attack walked straight into a prepared trap.
scenes.label: 4.2-inch mortar position west of Chorwon (May 1952)

lines: Second, firepower.
South Korean and UN guns fired more than 185,000 rounds.
The Chinese fired about 55,000.

visual.note: Shells fired · per ROK and U.S. records

lines: Third, a commander's instinct for handling his reserves.
General Kim sent in a fresh regiment before the one in the line could collapse.
He never gave the Chinese a moment to catch their breath.
Fourth, a South Korean army that had remade itself.
Barely a year earlier, ROK units had often crumbled before Chinese offensives.
Now, after intense retraining, that same army stopped the elite 38th Army head-on.
scenes.label: ROK troops in training (Jan 1952)

lines: According to South Korean records, the 9th Division suffered 3,422 casualties.
Chinese casualties are put at over 14,000, though Chinese sources give a figure of 6,700.
Behind every one of those numbers was someone's son, someone's brother.
After this battle, the ROK 9th Division earned a new name: the 'White Horse Division.'
That name remains the symbol of the division to this day.
scenes.label: ROK 9th Division today (2008)

chapter.title: IN THE NAME OF THE WHITE HORSE

lines: Then, on July 27th, 1953, the Armistice Agreement was signed.
White Horse Hill was left just as it was, inside the Demilitarized Zone.
South of the hill, a memorial now honors the sacrifices of those days.
scenes.label: White Horse Hill battle memorial

lines: Even today, the remains of the war dead are still being recovered in this area.
scenes.label: Recovering remains at White Horse Hill · ROK MND

lines: A hill just 395 meters high.
Beneath that number, thousands of young lives lie at rest.
scenes.label: ROK soldier (Mar 1952)

lines: A mountain stripped as white as a horse.
And those who held it to the very end were the ones who would not step back.

visual.title: What White Horse Hill Left Behind

items.text: A hill stripped white as a horse
Held by those who would not step back
